items.stem: The Transition Towns movement began in which town?
items.answer: Totnes, England

items.stem: A student claims: "Fairtrade guarantees farmers escape poverty." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Premiums help, but certification costs, small volumes sold at Fairtrade prices and low productivity limit benefits.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain how civil society can influence TNCs.
items.answer: NGO campaigns, boycotts, investigations and social media pressure damage brand reputation, pushing TNCs to adopt codes of conduct, supply-chain audits and Fairtrade sourcing, e.g. after Rana Plaza (the Bangladesh Accord). items.stem:
Refer to the data below.

Data: in a local multiplier study, £100 spent with a local supplier generated £176 for the local economy, while £100 spent with a non-local chain generated £136.

Explain why local spending generates a higher multiplier.
items.answer: Local firms employ local people, buy from local suppliers and keep profits in the area, so more money is re-spent locally.
items.markingKey: Local firms employ local people, buy from local suppliers and keep profits in the area, so more money is re-spent locally. Award 1 mark per valid point or correct step, up to [2]; data quoted must include units; points must be drawn from the resource.

items.stem: Briefly describe the Bangladesh Accord on Fire and Building Safety and explain what it reveals about civil society pressure on TNCs.
items.answer: After the 2013 Rana Plaza collapse, over 200 brands signed a legally binding agreement on factory inspections. Campaigns by unions and NGOs forced changes in supply-chain standards.
items.markingKey: Context (After the 2013 Rana Plaza collapse, over 200 brands signed a legally binding agreement on factory inspections.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Campaigns by unions and NGOs forced changes in supply-chain standards. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to civil society pressure on TNCs.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that anti-globalisation movements have been successful in changing global interactions?
items.answer: They have influenced standards and debate, but have not reversed globalisation.

items.stem: Define the term "Fairtrade".
items.answer: A certification system guaranteeing producers in developing countries minimum prices and a social premium
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a certification system guaranteeing producers in developing countries minimum prices and a social premium. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between free trade and Fairtrade.
items.answer: Free trade removes barriers so market prices decide trade; Fairtrade sets minimum prices and premiums to protect producers from low world prices.
items.markingKey: Free trade removes barriers so market prices decide trade; Fairtrade sets minimum prices and premiums to protect producers from low world prices. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between anti-globalisation and alter-globalisation.
items.answer: Anti-globalisation rejects many aspects of global integration; alter-globalisation accepts global connections but seeks fairer, more democratic and sustainable forms.

items.stem: Examine the reasons why localism is an effective response to the negative effects of globalisation in some places but not in others.
items.answer: local multiplier, identity, lower food miles in some cases; community resilience
items.markingKey: Paper 3 (a) indicative content: local multiplier, identity, lower food miles in some cases; community resilience; small scale; higher costs; local currencies often fail; cannot replace global supply chains for most goods. Markbands [12]: 10-12 detailed, accurate explanation with well-developed, located examples and clear links between factors; 7-9 accurate explanation, examples partly developed; 4-6 some relevant knowledge, mostly descriptive; 1-3 little relevant knowledge.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A limit on the quantity of a good that can be imported"?
items.answer: quota
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of quota.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A loose coalition of groups opposing aspects of corporate globalisation, such as free trade rules, TNC power and inequality"?
items.answer: anti-globalisation movement
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of anti-globalisation movement.

items.stem: Define the term "hashtag activism".
items.answer: Campaigns organised around a hashtag, e.g. #MeToo, #FridaysForFuture, #BringBackOurGirls
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: campaigns organised around a hashtag, e.g. #MeToo, #FridaysForFuture, #BringBackOurGirls. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between free trade and protectionism.
items.answer: Free trade removes tariffs and quotas so goods move freely; protectionism imposes barriers to shield domestic producers.
items.markingKey: Free trade removes tariffs and quotas so goods move freely; protectionism imposes barriers to shield domestic producers. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between Fairtrade and free trade.
items.answer: Free trade removes barriers so market prices decide trade; Fairtrade sets minimum prices and premiums to protect producers from low world prices.
items.markingKey: Free trade removes barriers so market prices decide trade; Fairtrade sets minimum prices and premiums to protect producers from low world prices. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why some critics describe online activism as slacktivism.
items.answer: Liking or sharing posts requires little effort or risk and may give a feeling of participation without changing policies; attention may fade quickly.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Liking or sharing posts requires little effort or risk and may give a feeling of participation without changing policies; attention may fade quickly. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Nia writes: "Border walls stop irregular migration." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: They redirect routes, raise smuggling costs and dangers, but do not stop migration driven by economic and political factors.
items.markingKey: They redirect routes, raise smuggling costs and dangers, but do not stop migration driven by economic and political factors. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain how civil society can influence TNCs.
items.answer: NGO campaigns, boycotts, investigations and social media pressure damage brand reputation, pushing TNCs to adopt codes of conduct, supply-chain audits and Fairtrade sourcing, e.g. after Rana Plaza (the Bangladesh Accord).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: NGO campaigns, boycotts, investigations and social media pressure damage brand reputation, pushing TNCs to adopt codes of conduct, supply-chain audits and Fairtrade sourcing, e.g. after Rana Plaza (the Bangladesh Accord). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Sana writes: "Technology always strengthens democracy." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Governments also use technology for surveillance, censorship and disinformation.
items.markingKey: Governments also use technology for surveillance, censorship and disinformation. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Between 2000 and 2012 the merchandise exports of a copper-exporting South American country changed from 110.3 to 120.8 US$ billion. Calculate the percentage change over the period.
items.markingKey: M1 (new − old) ÷ old × 100 = (120.8 − 110.3) ÷ 110.3 × 100; A1 +9.5% (sign or "increase/decrease" required).

items.stem:
The following information is provided.

Table: Fairtrade retail sales (€ billion, global, approximate) - 2004: 0.8; 2010: 4.4; 2016: 7.9; 2022: 12.0.

Suggest one reason for the growth.
items.answer: Rising ethical consumerism, campaigns by NGOs and supermarket adoption of Fairtrade products.
items.markingKey: Rising ethical consumerism, campaigns by NGOs and supermarket adoption of Fairtrade products. Award 1 mark per valid point or correct step, up to [3]; data quoted must include units; points must be drawn from the resource.

items.stem: A data table shows the inward FDI stock of a Latin American middle-income country: 1995 - 205.4 US$ billion; 2010 - 282.8 US$ billion. Calculate the percentage change over the period.
items.markingKey: M1 (new − old) ÷ old × 100 = (282.8 − 205.4) ÷ 205.4 × 100; A1 +37.7% (sign or "increase/decrease" required).

items.stem: With reference to the US-China trade war, explain how it illustrates protectionism.
items.answer: Tariffs from 2018 covered hundreds of billions of dollars of goods, and US soybean exports to China fell by about 75% in 2018. Tariff escalation disrupted trade flows and shifted supply chains.
items.markingKey: Context (Tariffs from 2018 covered hundreds of billions of dollars of goods, and US soybean exports to China fell by about 75% in 2018.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Tariff escalation disrupted trade flows and shifted supply chains. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to protectionism.

items.stem: Suggest one benefit and one limitation of local currencies.
items.answer: Benefit: keeps spending within local businesses, increasing the local multiplier; limitation: limited acceptance and use, so many have closed (Bristol Pound 2021).
items.markingKey: Benefit: keeps spending within local businesses, increasing the local multiplier; limitation: limited acceptance and use, so many have closed (Bristol Pound 2021).

items.stem: With reference to Fridays for Future, explain how it illustrates transnational activism through social media.
items.answer: Greta Thunberg's 2018 school strike grew into global strikes involving about 6 million people in September 2019. Digital networks spread a local protest worldwide.
items.markingKey: Context (Greta Thunberg's 2018 school strike grew into global strikes involving about 6 million people in September 2019.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Digital networks spread a local protest worldwide. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to transnational activism through social media.

items.stem: Suggest why Brexit affected trade between Great Britain and Northern Ireland.
items.answer: The Northern Ireland Protocol (later the Windsor Framework) kept Northern Ireland in the EU single market for goods to avoid a hard border with Ireland, so checks were introduced on goods crossing the Irish Sea.
items.markingKey: The Northern Ireland Protocol (later the Windsor Framework) kept Northern Ireland in the EU single market for goods to avoid a hard border with Ireland, so checks were introduced on goods crossing the Irish Sea.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that social media has made transnational activism more effective?
items.answer: Social media makes activism faster and wider, but lasting change needs offline organisation.

items.answer: job competition, wages, public services; deindustrialised regions voted Leave

items.stem: "Localism is an effective response to the negative effects of globalisation." To what extent do you agree with this statement? In your answer, consider the perspectives of different places and scales.
items.answer: Localism brings community benefits but is a limited response to global forces.
